name: Treaty with the Osage, 1825
nations: Osage (Wazhazhe) Nation, then the Great and Little Osage
promises: A reservation fifty miles wide running west from a point twenty-five miles west of Missouri, for the Osage so long as they chose to occupy it, surveyed at United States expense (Article 2).
An annuity of $7,000 a year for twenty years, in money, goods, provisions or animals at the Osage's option (Article 3).
Cattle, hogs, fowls, oxen, carts, farming tools, farm helpers, a blacksmith and a house for each of the four principal chiefs (Article 4).
Fifty-four sections to be sold to fund schools for Osage children (Article 6).
Protection, and a guarantee forever of free navigation of the waterways in the ceded country (Article 11).

breaches.what: After the Indian Claims Commission held in 1968 that the Osage had original Indian title to the lands ceded by this treaty and by the treaty of September 25, 1818, and before any value was tried, the Osage Nation and the United States settled this claim together with three others by compromise for a net $13,250,000.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Osage Nation v. United States, Dockets 105, 106, 107 and 108, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement, September 3, 1970 (23 Ind. Cl. Comm. 447); title order in Dockets 106 and 107, September 1968 (19 Ind. Cl. Comm. 447)

source.title: Osage Nation v. United States, Dockets 105-108, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement (September 3, 1970)
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

landTaken: The Commission held that the lands described in its Finding 29 in Dockets 106 and 107 were held by the Osage by original Indian title and ceded by this treaty; the compromise findings describe the 1818 and 1825 cessions together as Royce's Cession 97 and a portion of Cession 123, in Missouri, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Kansas.
compensation: No value or consideration for the 1825 cession was ever adjudicated. The 1970 compromise of $13,250,000 covered Dockets 105 (the 1808 cession), 106 and 107 (the 1818 and 1825 cessions) and 108 (attorney fees paid from Osage funds) without dividing the sum by treaty.
today: The claim ended with the 1970 compromise. Under the 1825 treaty itself, no court or Commission finding that a specific promise was not kept was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Osage Nation teaches that the Treaty of 1825 was devastating, that William Clark later called it the hardest treaty he ever made on the Indians, and that the promise to keep the southern Kansas strip for the Osage alone was broken when the government let settlers move in.

openQuestions: The day of the Dockets 106-107 title order is illegible in the scan; the collection lists it as September 10, 1968 and the compromise findings as September 20, 1968. Neither is recorded as the breach date.

treaties.json lists both 'The Osage Nation, Oklahoma' and 'Osage Tribe, Oklahoma' as present-day tribes for this entry; they appear to be one nation. It also links Royce Area 475, which was not checked against Royce. Not edited.
Whether the Article 6 school lands were sold and the fund applied, and whether the twenty annuities were paid, was not researched.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 8): plain.promised said the reservation was 'in present Kansas', which the file does not source; reworded to 'west of Missouri' as Article 2 says. Breach, dates, $13,250,000 and the 1968 title order (OSU ids 1352, 2223) confirmed.

plain.promised: A reservation west of Missouri, $7,000 a year for twenty years, livestock, tools and farm help, and land sold to pay for Osage schools, in return for Osage land in Missouri, Arkansas and beyond.
plain.happened: In 1968 the Indian Claims Commission held the Osage had owned the land this treaty took. The land's value was never decided.
plain.today: In 1970 the Osage Nation settled this claim and three others together for $13,250,000, without a finding on this treaty's price.
